title.en: Tapestry, Grotesques de Berain, The Elephant
title.sv: Tapet: Grotesques de Berain med motiv Elefanten

identity.artistOrCulture: Jean-Baptiste Monnoyer and Jean Bérain I; Manufacture de Beauvais

availabilityEvidence.boundary: The official catalogue confirmed display at research time; future display remains mutable.

works.coreValue: One member of Nationalmuseum's four-piece NMK 299A–D/2016 group from Carl Piper's documented Beauvais tapestry order, useful for explaining French-Swedish luxury exchange, patron-specific adaptation and the later dispersal and partial reunion of an ensemble.
selectionSignals: The object page identifies NMK 299A/2016 as part of NMK 299A–D/2016 and records four tapestries acquired by Nationalmuseum in 2016.
Nationalmuseum's Art Bulletin identifies the four museum pieces individually as The Elephant, The Offering to Bacchus, Peacock and The Offering to Pan.

Correspondence between Daniel Cronström and Nicodemus Tessin the Younger documents Piper's order and identifies Monnoyer in connection with the series; the museum account assigns Bérain a new border design.
The scholarly article says Les Grotesques was woven in variants around 50 times over more than 40 years and that more than 150 individual tapestries are known, so the motif type is not globally rare.
Its strongest value is the documented Swedish commission and surviving four-piece group, not uniqueness of the Elephant motif.
routeSignals: Treat as one object within a four-piece Nationalmuseum group, not as the entire original suite

multi_part_work.evidence: NMK 299A/2016 is The Elephant and one of the four Nationalmuseum accessions NMK 299A–D/2016. The museum article names B as The Offering to Bacchus, C as Peacock and D as The Offering to Pan. The historical set was larger and later dispersed, so A must not stand for the full original suite.
multi_part_work.remainingUncertainty: The object-page narrative describes an original set of six, while the scholarly article reports the group traced to George Jorck as seven tapestries and a fragment; neither statement turns the four museum accessions into a complete original set.

attribution_or_date_conflict.evidence: The official object record displays 1695, while the Nationalmuseum Art Bulletin captions the four works circa 1696–99 and says the tapestries arrived toward the end of 1699. The catalogue narrative treats 1695 as the commission year. The object record lists Monnoyer and Bérain as designers, while its research narrative identifies Monnoyer for the suite patterns and Bérain for the border; the Bulletin describes the work as after designs by both.
attribution_or_date_conflict.remainingUncertainty: Use 1695 only as the catalogue display date or commission anchor; use circa 1696–99 for execution when following the Art Bulletin. Do not collapse the composition and border roles into an unsupported single attribution formula.

cross_source_synthesis.evidence: The official catalogue supplies current identity, display and acquisition data; the Nationalmuseum Art Bulletin supplies the component list, comparison population, date range and provenance reconstruction.
cross_source_synthesis.remainingUncertainty: The exact original-set count and exact execution year remain bounded as stated above.

comparisonEvidence.comparisonCategory: Beauvais Les Grotesques tapestries after Monnoyer/Bérain designs
comparisonEvidence.nearestComparators: Other subjects and variants in the same widely woven Les Grotesques design family, including the three companion Nationalmuseum accessions and known complete sets and individual tapestries elsewhere.
comparisonEvidence.sharedCoreValue: They share the Beauvais grotesque design family, wool-and-silk medium and adaptable compositions.
comparisonEvidence.decisiveDifference: This example's selection value lies in its connection to Piper's unusually well-documented Swedish order and its membership in the four works acquired together by Nationalmuseum, rather than in a unique motif or singular surviving type.
comparisonEvidence.knownQuantityBoundary: The Art Bulletin reports the design woven around 50 times and more than 150 individual tapestries known; it does not establish a worldwide survival count for Piper's exact original suite.

scoreEvidence: The documented patronage, cross-border commission, preserved ensemble relationship and correspondence support historical-cultural and collection-line importance.
The broad survival of the design family defeats a motif-level rarity claim, and exact Piper-suite survival boundaries remain incomplete; classify as important rather than rare.

identity.artistOrCulture: Unknown; former attribution Jonas Frisk workshop

availabilityEvidence.boundary: The official catalogue confirmed display at research time; future display remains mutable.

works.coreValue: A securely identified member of a seven-piece museum-held furniture group from Sweden's former foreign-minister residence, preserving institutional setting, French period silk and ensemble relationships despite an unknown maker.
selectionSignals: The official record identifies the maker as unknown and Jonas Frisk workshop only as a former attribution; selection must not present Frisk as maker.
The original group comprised at least 13 pieces: two sofas, eight armchairs, two banquettes and a mirror.
Seven pieces transferred to Nationalmuseum are one sofa, four armchairs, one banquette and the mirror, catalogued as NMK 109–115/2013.

The building served as the foreign minister's official residence and a venue for official functions until the early 1960s; the original room retains silk wallpaper matching the upholstery's red shade.
Storage probably preserved the original upholstery; probability wording must be retained.
routeSignals: Anchor the 1800–1870 furniture and institutional-interior line
Present as one chair within a seven-piece museum group

multi_part_work.evidence: NMK 110/2013 is one armchair within NMK 109–115/2013, the seven pieces transferred to Nationalmuseum. The historical ensemble comprised at least 13 pieces, so neither this chair nor the seven museum pieces should be called the complete original ensemble.
multi_part_work.remainingUncertainty: The official page establishes a minimum original count, not a closed global survival inventory.

attribution_or_date_conflict.evidence: The current official record says Made by: Unknown and separately records Jonas Frisk workshop as Former attribution.
attribution_or_date_conflict.remainingUncertainty: No current maker is identified; the former attribution must remain historical and cannot be revived as authorship.

comparisonEvidence.nearestComparators: The suite in the Lantern Room at Rosendal Palace, completed around 1829.
comparisonEvidence.sharedCoreValue: The official account says both suites use the same French silk and have an identical basic shape.
comparisonEvidence.decisiveDifference: Rosendal uses hand-carved ornament and real gold leaf; the foreign-minister-residence suite uses cast lead ornament and a gilt effect made with metal foil and bronzing.
comparisonEvidence.knownQuantityBoundary: At least 13 pieces in the original residence suite; seven are held by Nationalmuseum. No worldwide count is established.

scoreEvidence: Institutional provenance, surviving ensemble structure, matching original-room context and period upholstery support historical-cultural and collection-line importance.
The Rosendal parallel supplies a close substitute for formal comparison, and no global rarity hard-gate is met.
